//: RECOMMENDED PERMISSIONS for AgenTeX (Browser Testing + Azure DevOps task estimation). Plugin settings.json cannot carry permission rules, so copy the blocks below into your PROJECT .claude/settings.json (merge with any existing 'permissions'). These pre-approve the commands a run actually issues, gate destructive ones behind a prompt, and deny secret reads and edits to your application's source.
//notes: allow > Bash(node:*) — the plugin does its non-browser work through bundled node scripts (preflight.js, init_run.js, run_api.js, run_db.js, ask_kb.js, session.js, fetch_baseline.js, make_html_report.js, create-bug.js). Without this rule a single test run stops for a permission prompt at every one of them. To tighten it, replace this entry with 'Bash(node <absolute path to the installed plugin>/skills:*)' — run /plugin to see that path — which allows only the plugin's own scripts.

allow > az rules — no tracker flow uses az: bug filing, estimation, test design, and test-plan updates all run through bundled node scripts over the Azure DevOps REST API (already covered by the Bash(node:*) rule), so no az permission prompt can occur there. The az rules below serve only the azure-integration skill (the Azure resource plane: login, discovery, App Service, Storage, Key Vault, AKS).

deny > Bash flag order defeats prefix matching: a rule matches the START of the command, so 'Bash(rm -rf:*)' alone never sees 'rm -fr' or 'rm -r -f'. Each spelling needs its own entry, and on Windows 'Remove-Item' is denied outright because its -Recurse/-Force flags can appear in any order after it.

deny > Edit(./src/**) alone does not protect your application: Write and MultiEdit reach the same files by a different tool, so all three are listed. Point them at wherever your app's source actually lives — if it is not ./src, these rules protect nothing. The agent never needs to write to your application; it only writes under test/ and executions/.

deny > secret files: the plugin's design is that config and catalog files name env vars and the values live in your shell or .env, which the bundled scripts read themselves. Nothing in a run needs the agent to READ a .env, a key or a certificate, so those reads are denied rather than trusted.

ask > curl and sqlcmd are one prompt each, on purpose. API and DB steps run through the api-integration / db-integration runners, which keep credentials in the environment and off the command line; a bare curl or sqlcmd is either an ad-hoc check worth confirming, or a way for data to leave the machine.
